tldr: This paper presents RoboEdit, a video editing suite that transforms human manipulation videos into videos of a target robot hand while preserving the background and object dynamics, and also estimates 3D hand trajectories. Trained on an automatically built large-scale dataset of 14 million frames, it enables high-fidelity video generation and motion control on real-world robots.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of RoboEdit-Trans. Adapting a pretrained diffusion backbone to specific robot hand geometries and kinematics via LoRA and residual adapters, and extracting 3D hand trajectories from generated robot videos using the 3D Robot-State Decoder.
overview:
In robot manipulation learning, video data provides an exceptionally strong supervisory signal because it captures contacts, object dynamics, and camera viewpoints all at once. However, collecting data on real robots is costly, and the data cannot be directly reused when the hand morphology or degrees of freedom change—an issue known as the embodiment barrier. Meanwhile, massive amounts of human manipulation videos exist in the wild, but differences in appearance and kinematic structures have made them difficult to use directly as training data.

To bridge this gap, the authors asked: "Can we automatically edit human manipulation videos by replacing only the human hands with a target robot hand in a physically plausible way?" This idea led to the development of RoboEdit. First, they built RoboEdit-ADC, an automatic data generation pipeline that reconstructs 3D hand-object-camera interactions from monocular RGB videos and retargets them to robots using depth normalization and physics-guided optimization. This enabled the creation of RoboEdit-14M, a paired dataset covering 7 robot embodiments across 14 million frames. Using this large-scale dataset, they trained RoboEdit-Trans, a video editing model with LoRA and residual adapters for multi-embodiment adaptation, along with a 3D Robot-State Decoder to recover camera-frame 3D hand trajectories from the generated videos.

In experiments, RoboEdit significantly outperformed existing video editing baselines in visual quality and physical consistency. Furthermore, using the 3D trajectories predicted from the generated videos, downstream policies successfully performed grasping and manipulation tasks on YCB objects in both simulation and on a real Franka Panda robot. This opens a practical pathway to turning vast amounts of human videos directly into visual and motion learning data for robotics.
contributions: Proposed RoboEdit, an integrated suite that converts human manipulation videos into robot manipulation videos while maintaining backgrounds and object dynamics, and simultaneously recovers 3D hand trajectories.

Developed RoboEdit-ADC, an automatic pipeline that reconstructs 3D interactions from monocular RGB videos and synthesizes high-quality paired data through depth normalization and physics-guided retargeting.
Constructed RoboEdit-14M, the first large-scale paired dataset comprising 7 robot embodiments and 174K video pairs totaling 14.1 million frames.

Combined LoRA and residual adapters on top of a shared diffusion backbone to simultaneously achieve appearance and kinematic adaptation across diverse robots alongside accurate 3D hand state recovery suitable for real-robot control.

sections.heading: Turning Massive Human Videos Directly into Robot Experience
sections.summary: To address the cost and hardware specificity of robot video collection, this work introduces RoboEdit to transform human manipulation videos into robot videos. It consists of an automatic data generation pipeline, a 14M-frame paired dataset, and a video editing model with cross-embodiment adaptation and 3D state recovery.
sections.details:
In robot manipulation learning, videos rich in contact events, object motion, camera viewpoints, and environmental context serve as an invaluable source of supervision. However, collecting video data on physical robots is exceedingly expensive, and when robot hand morphologies or kinematics differ, the collected data cannot be transferred directly. As a result, existing datasets remain confined to limited sets of objects and environments.

In contrast, human-object interaction videos are abundant online and in existing datasets. The primary obstacle preventing their direct use in robot training is the morphological mismatch between human and robot bodies. Prior studies have leveraged human videos for feature pretraining or coarse hand tracking, but directly converting human videos into physically plausible manipulation videos executed by a specific target robot remained unexplored.

To tackle this, the authors propose RoboEdit, an integrated suite comprising three key components:
- RoboEdit-ADC: An automatic data creation pipeline that reconstructs 3D hand-object interactions from monocular RGB videos, applies depth correction and physical optimization, and synthesizes robot videos.
- RoboEdit-14M: The first large-scale paired dataset spanning 7 robot embodiments, containing 174K pairs and 14.1 million frames.
- RoboEdit-Trans: A video editing engine built on a shared video diffusion model, using LoRA and residual adapters to adapt to each robot's appearance and kinematics while estimating 3D hand trajectories from the generated videos.

This makes it possible to achieve visual consistency while simultaneously extracting 3D motion supervision directly usable for downstream reinforcement learning and real-world robot control.

captions.F3: Examples from the large-scale RoboEdit-14M dataset. Everyday manipulation tasks are retargeted across seven robot embodiments, ranging from multi-fingered dexterous hands to parallel-jaw grippers.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of Human Video Learning, Retargeting, and Video Editing
sections.summary: The paper contextualizes its approach within three research areas: robot learning from human videos, human-to-robot retargeting, and diffusion-based video editing. RoboEdit is pioneering in achieving both full video synthesis and dense 3D motion recovery within a single framework.
sections.details:
This work sits at the intersection of three domains across robotics and computer vision.

### Robot Learning from Human Videos
Numerous studies have explored learning visual representations, value functions for imitation or reinforcement learning, and affordance maps from human videos. However, these methods typically extract intermediate representations or sparse trajectories, falling short of synthesizing complete manipulation videos alongside dense 3D motion for target robots.

### Human-to-Robot Retargeting
Mapping human hand motions onto robot hands with different kinematic structures has long been studied in teleoperation and related fields. Recent advances incorporate contact constraints and physical plausibility into optimization routines, but their outputs remain restricted to joint angles and trajectories without producing natural visual scenes that include backgrounds and objects.

### Human-to-Robot Video Editing
Recent advances in diffusion models have significantly pushed the boundaries of object-replacement video editing. However, existing video editing methods assume that the agent's morphology and kinematics remain unchanged. When replacing human hands with robot hands, not only does appearance shift, but finger counts, joint limits, and contact dynamics change fundamentally, causing standard video editing techniques to introduce severe artifacts and physical implausibility. RoboEdit overcomes this hurdle by combining physics simulator-based retargeting with cross-embodiment adaptation.

sections.heading: Simultaneously Generating Physically Consistent Videos and 3D Trajectories
sections.summary: This section details the architecture and modules of RoboEdit: 3D reconstruction and physical retargeting in RoboEdit-ADC, cross-embodiment adaptation in RoboEdit-Trans, and the 3D Robot-State Decoder.
sections.details:
Given a human-object manipulation video $v^h_{1:T}$ and a target robot embodiment $e$, RoboEdit aims to synthesize a physically plausible manipulation video $\hat{v}^{r,e}_{1:T}$ within the same scene, while simultaneously predicting the 3D hand state trajectory $\hat{q}^{e}_{1:T}$ of the robot hand.

### 3.1 RoboEdit-ADC: Automatic Data Creation Pipeline
To construct paired training videos, 3D scenes are reconstructed from monocular videos and composited:
- 3D Interaction Reconstruction: HaMeR reconstructs hand meshes, SAM 2 segments object masks, TRELLIS and FoundationPose extract 3D object meshes and 6D pose trajectories, and VGGT estimates camera intrinsics, extrinsics, and depth. To resolve depth ambiguities and scale mismatches typical of monocular estimation, the estimated palm joints are back-projected onto depth maps, correcting the hand's 3D translation via isotropic scaling centered at the camera origin.
- Physics-Guided Retargeting: Initial joint trajectories are generated using SPIDER-based inverse kinematics (IK) for multi-fingered hands or geometric optimization for two- and three-finger grippers. Then, physical optimization is performed using a compound objective function combining tracking loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{track}}$, temporal smoothness loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{temp}}$, penetration penalty $\mathcal{L}_{\text{geo}}$ based on MuJoCo collision detection and signed distance fields, and contact loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{contact}}$ that pulls fingertips toward object surfaces within a threshold.
- Robot Video Synthesis: MiniMax-Remover inpaints hands and objects to extract clean backgrounds, onto which rendered passes of retargeted robots and objects are composited.

### 3.2 RoboEdit-Trans: Video Editing Model and 3D State Decoder
RoboEdit-Trans is built upon Wan2.1-VACE (1.3B parameters) from NovaEdit.
- Cross-Embodiment Adaptation: After pretraining a shared human-to-robot backbone, the base weights are frozen. Light LoRA layers adapt to each robot's spatio-temporal dynamics, while residual bottleneck adapters capture fine hand geometry, enabling multi-robot support with minimal added parameters.
- 3D Robot-State Decoder: Because generated videos lack explicit 3D coordinates, this decoder recovers them. A shared ResNet-34 feature extractor combined with robot-specific prediction heads estimates 2D palm anchors, 2D fingertips, and normalized joint angles per frame. The SQPnP algorithm deterministically solves for camera-frame 3D wrist poses, followed by a temporal Transformer that ensures physical consistency and sequence smoothness.

### 3.3 RoboEdit-14M: Dataset Scale and Diversity
RoboEdit-14M includes 145K real-world video pairs sourced from five public datasets (including DexYCB and HOT3D) and 29K synthetic scene pairs with randomized backgrounds generated via RoboEngine. In total, the dataset contains 174K pairs (14.1 million frames) across 7 robot hands (such as Inspire, XHand, and Franka Panda).

sections.heading: Benchmarking Video Quality and Succeeding on Real Hardware
sections.summary: RoboEdit achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and temporal consistency across a 300-sample benchmark compared to existing video editing baselines. Furthermore, the decoded 3D trajectories successfully drove object manipulation in simulation and on a physical Franka Panda robot.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup
The evaluation was conducted on a test set of 300 unseen manipulation sequences. Baselines included state-of-the-art video editing and generation models such as VACE, UniVideo, VINO, Kiwi-Edit, OmniWeaving, and ReCo. Visual quality was evaluated using SSIM, LPIPS, editing-region LPIPS, and background SSIM, alongside VBench and OpenVE-Bench metrics for overall video quality and temporal consistency.

### Qualitative and Quantitative Results
Qualitative comparisons (Figure F4) reveal that baseline methods often leave residual human hand parts or generate distorted robot fingers. In contrast, RoboEdit-Trans cleanly replaces hands with target robot effectors (both multi-fingered hands and parallel grippers) while strictly preserving background fidelity and object trajectories. Quantitative results in Table 2 demonstrate that RoboEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance in reconstruction fidelity (LPIPS and SSIM) and local editing accuracy against reference videos.

### Ablation Studies
Ablations on architectural components showed that both LoRA and residual adapters contributed to performance gains. The residual adapter, in particular, was crucial for capturing robot hand geometry. Combining both components delivered the best results across all metrics.

### Simulation and Real-Robot Transfer
To verify whether decoded 3D trajectories could directly drive robot control, manipulation tasks on YCB objects were conducted in the Genesis simulator. A residual PPO policy was trained to compensate for tracking errors around the predicted trajectories, achieving success rates of 71% for the Panda gripper and 62% for the multi-fingered XHand across 512 randomized environments. Furthermore, deploying the same controller onto a physical 7-DoF Franka Panda robot demonstrated stable grasping and manipulation of real YCB objects by tracking the decoded 3D trajectories.

sections.heading: A New Foundation for Converting Human Videos into Robot Experience
sections.summary: The paper concludes by summarizing RoboEdit's ability to transform human hand manipulation videos into physically plausible robot videos and 3D hand trajectories, opening a scalable path to convert abundant human video data into robot training assets.
sections.details:
This paper presented RoboEdit, a framework that converts human manipulation videos into high-fidelity, physically consistent robot manipulation videos and 3D hand trajectories.

Through the automated data generation pipeline RoboEdit-ADC, depth ambiguities and contact artifacts in monocular RGB videos were eliminated to build RoboEdit-14M, a massive 14.1M-frame dataset. The editing engine RoboEdit-Trans then demonstrated flexible adaptation across diverse robot embodiments and recovered 3D trajectories ready for real-world control within a unified pipeline.

Experiments confirmed state-of-the-art visual editing performance and proved the downstream utility of decoded 3D motion signals through successful manipulation in simulation and on a real Franka Panda robot. This research establishes a powerful foundation for transforming the vast wealth of human videos on the web into scalable, actionable robot experience.

sections.heading: Implementation Details: Physics Optimization, State Decoder, and Controllers
sections.summary: This section covers technical specifications detailed in the appendix, including depth scaling, contact loss thresholds, the multi-task loss for the 3D decoder, and the mathematical formulation of the residual RL controller used in simulation and real-robot experiments.
sections.details:
### Depth Normalization and Physical Loss Design (Appendix A)
- Depth Alignment: Stable wrist and finger base joints (palm anchors $\mathcal{A}$) are selected from the MANO model. The ratio $\alpha = \bar{z}^D / \bar{z}^H$ between the median depth from the VGGT depth map $\bar{z}^D$ and the median HaMeR depth $\bar{z}^H$ is computed. Multiplying the hand's camera-frame translation by $\alpha$ performs isotropic scaling, matching the physical metric depth while preserving 2D screen projections.
- Physics Losses: Signed distance field penalties prevent mesh interpenetration below a clearance threshold $\delta=5\,\text{mm}$. Contact constraints engage when the fingertip-to-surface distance drops below $\tau_k \in [2\,\text{cm}, 6\,\text{cm}]$. To prevent contact chattering, a hysteresis threshold of $+1\,\text{cm}$ is added for detachment, and only contact intervals lasting at least 10 consecutive frames are retained.

### 3D Robot-State Decoder Architecture and Losses (Appendix B)
Using a ResNet-34 feature pyramid, the decoder predicts 8 2D palm anchors, up to 5 2D fingertips, palm-frame 3D fingertips, normalized joint angles, and camera intrinsics in parallel. Training utilizes a multi-task objective comprising anchor loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{anchor}}$, spatial geometric loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{spa}}$, and temporal smoothness loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{tmp}}$. Camera-frame 3D wrist poses are computed deterministically via SQPnP.

### Robot Control via Residual Reinforcement Learning (Appendix E)
The decoded 3D trajectory $\tau^h = \{h^{\star}_t\}_{t=1}^T$ serves as reference. Given nominal joint commands $q^{\text{IK}}_t$ from inverse kinematics, a PPO-trained residual policy $\pi_\phi$ outputs corrective actions $a_t \in [-1, 1]^7$ scaled by $\rho_{\text{act}}=0.02\,\text{rad}$:
$$q^{\text{cmd}}_t = \operatorname{clip}(q^{\text{IK}}_t + \rho_{\text{act}} a_t, q_{\min}, q_{\max})$$
In the Genesis simulator across 18 YCB objects, a single policy proved robust against randomized object poses and positions, transferring seamlessly to achieve reliable grasping on a physical Franka Panda arm.

takeaways: Converting human videos into robot videos hinges on creating large-scale paired datasets via video inpainting and physics-guided retargeting that preserve background and object dynamics.
Directly retargeting monocular 3D reconstructions causes floating or penetration; depth-map palm scaling and physics/mesh-based contact optimization are essential.
Freezing the base video diffusion model while combining LoRA (appearance/motion) and residual adapters (hand geometry) provides an effective strategy for multi-embodiment domain adaptation.
Decoding camera-frame 3D joint and wrist poses directly from generated videos creates a bridge from video generation to trajectory tracking and residual RL on physical robots.
limitations: Inference relies on an external model (a fine-tuned Qwen-Image-Edit) for keyframe generation rather than operating as a fully end-to-end single network.
Evaluation metrics face challenges: background SSIM can penalize legitimate mask-boundary changes caused by volume and shape differences between human and robot hands.
Severe occlusions, extremely fast object movements, or complex geometric interlocks between hands and objects can cause 3D mesh tracking or depth estimation failures that propagate downstream.
